talks.title: RomHack 2025 - James “albinowax” Kettle - HTTP/1.1 Must Die! The Desync Endgame
talks.teaser: Explores romHack 2025 - James “albinowax” Kettle - HTTP/1.1 Must Die! The Desync Endgame and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
HTTP/1.1 Desync Endgame

James Kettle revisits four years of HTTP request-smuggling research expecting minor edge cases, but finds the problem worsening. HTTP/1.1 cannot reliably separate requests; tiny parser differences between frontends and backends enable desyncs and often full site takeover.

Industry Response vs Reality

Deploying HTTP/2 upstream was the hoped-for fix, yet many stacks accept H2 from clients then downgrade to H1 toward backends. Vendors added regex blocks that stop scanners and classic probes while leaving vulnerabilities exploitable—creating false confidence Kettle calls the “desync endgame.”

Cloudflare Case Study

A researcher’s smuggling test appeared blocked at Cloudflare’s cache edge yet still desynced inside Cloudflare infrastructure, potentially affecting masses of sites when static GET requests omitted cache busters. Kettle argues proxy chains that convert H2→H1→H2 amplify complexity built on a broken foundation.

Research Agenda

He plans new tooling, additional desync attack classes, and scrutiny of whether H2 truly succeeds H1—arguing upstream HTTP/1.1 must die and be proven insecure to drive change.

talks.title: RomHack 2025 - Denis Nagayuk (diversenok) - Attacking Assumptions Behind the Image Load Callbacks
talks.teaser: Examines romHack 2025 - Denis Nagayuk (diversenok) - Attacking Assumptions Behind the Image Load Callbacks and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Feature Overview

Denis Nagayuk (diversenok) of Hunt & Hackett examines Windows image-load notify routines used by Sysmon event 7, AV, and EDR tools to inspect DLL loads and enforce code-signing policies such as System Informer protections.

Callback Semantics

Drivers register via documented APIs receiving mapped image base, process ID, file name, and extended file-object pointers. Callbacks run synchronously after NtMapViewOfSection—post-operation—so images are visible to other threads while inspection runs; drivers cannot cancel loads cleanly without crashing callers.

Scope and Assumptions

The mechanism covers image-backed sections, not all executable private memory or data sections, which drives manual mapping evasion. Nagayuk formalizes OS and driver assumptions: files still exist, names remain queryable, and security products can open or hash images during callbacks.

Research Direction

He maps the file → file object → section → mapped image chain where mismatches create attack surface, aiming to violate those assumptions and show defenders where reliance on image-load callbacks breaks down.

talks.title: RomHack 2025 - Leon Jacobs - 7 Vulns in 7 Days: Breaking Bloatware Faster Than It’s Built
talks.teaser: Reviews romHack 2025 - Leon Jacobs - 7 Vulns in 7 Days: Breaking Bloatware Faster Than Its Built and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Bloatware research origin

Leon Jacobs recounts discovering ASUS DriverHub's local web server after a suspiciously fast reboot during gaming. He targeted ASUS DriverHub, MSI Center, Acer Control Center, and Razer Synapse 4—now patched—using Process Explorer, Binary Ninja, and Burp in VMs with installer anti-VM checks bypassed.

ASUS DriverHub attack path

ADU.exe listens on TCP 5300; the public site's JavaScript calls localhost APIs. Origin-header checks and POST body requirements were reverse-engineered from logs and minified JS, enabling unauthenticated reboot via /reboot with forged origin and JSON command payloads—a string-contains origin-validation flaw.

Broader pattern

Jacobs shows how OEM driver hub bloatware exposes privileged local HTTP APIs to browser-origin policies that are trivially bypassed. The week-long sprint yielded multiple CVEs across vendors, illustrating systemic risk in preinstalled manufacturer utilities that bridge web UIs to system-level actions.

talks.title: RomHack 2025 - Philippe Caturegli
talks.teaser: Evaluates romHack 2025 - Philippe Caturegli and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Domain Collisions Still Matter

Philippe Caturegli presents red-team research on domain name collisions—cases where internal corporate names collide with real, publicly registered TLDs. Despite ICANN studies dating to 2013, enterprises still suffer from choices made decades ago.

## WPAD Gone Wrong

During an IT services engagement, his team registered initech.lc, mirroring a fictional internal domain. Remote employees' browsers queried WPAD URLs like wpad.initech.lc through public DNS when home routers could not resolve internal names, letting attackers host malicious proxy configs.

## Internal AD Names vs. New gTLDs

Many organizations adopted short internal domains before new gTLDs existed. Active Directory cannot rename domains, leaving companies stuck with names now owned by strangers—enabling phishing, credential interception, and VPN bypass scenarios.

## ICANN Mitigations and Gaps

Caturegli reviews ICANN's name collision framework from JAS Global Advisors and discusses newer TLD quirks (including memorable examples like .zip). Defenders should audit internal namespaces, disable unsafe WPAD, and plan migrations where collisions create external trust boundaries.
